claim: Tristetraprolin (TTP) binds AU-rich elements in the untranslated-regions of many mRNAs encoding pro-inflammatory mediators, thereby accelerating their decay.
source: Tristetraprolin (TTP) is a critical negative immune regulator. It binds AU-rich elements in the untranslated-regions of many mRNAs encoding pro-inflammatory mediators, thereby accelerating their decay.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Galloway et al., 2016; Lai et al., 1999; Sedlyarov et al., 2016) and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: TTP is degraded by the proteasome through yet unidentified phosphorylation-controlled drivers.
source: A key but poorly understood mechanism of TTP regulation is its timely proteolytic removal: TTP is degraded by the proteasome through yet unidentified phosphorylation-controlled drivers.
evidence: This claim acknowledges a gap in knowledge and is supported by inference from existing literature about TTP degradation mechanisms.

claim: TTP is strongly lysine-ubiquitinated, which is required for its turnover.
source: Cellular assays showed that TTP is strongly lysine-ubiquitinated, which is required for its turnover.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cellular assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: The ubiquitin E3 ligase HUWE1 is a strong regulator of TTP proteasomal degradation.
source: A genetic screen identified the ubiquitin E3 ligase HUWE1 as a strong regulator of TTP proteasomal degradation
evidence: This claim is supported by data from a genetic screen described in the manuscript.

claim: HUWE1 controls TTP stability indirectly by regulating its phosphorylation.
source: which we found to control TTP stability indirectly by regulating its phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and inference from pharmacological and genetic experiments.

claim: HUWE1-regulated TTP phosphorylation and stability was independent of the previously characterized effects of MAPK-mediated S52/S178 phosphorylation.
source: Pharmacological assessment of multiple kinases revealed that HUWE1-regulated TTP phosphorylation and stability was independent of the previously characterized effects of MAPK-mediated S52/S178 phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological experiments with kinase inhibitors presented in the manuscript.

claim: HUWE1 function was dependent on phosphatase and E3 ligase binding sites identified in the TTP C-terminus.
source: HUWE1 function was dependent on phosphatase and E3 ligase binding sites identified in the TTP C-terminus.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from deletion mutant experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Phosphorylation of S52/S178 is critical for TTP stabilization at earlier times after pro-inflammatory stimulation.
source: Our findings indicate that while phosphorylation of S52/S178 is critical for TTP stabilization at earlier times after pro-inflammatory stimulation, phosphorylation of the TTP C-terminus controls its stability at later stages.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and builds on previously published findings.

claim: Phosphorylation of the TTP C-terminus controls its stability at later stages after pro-inflammatory stimulation.
source: Our findings indicate that while phosphorylation of S52/S178 is critical for TTP stabilization at earlier times after pro-inflammatory stimulation, phosphorylation of the TTP C-terminus controls its stability at later stages.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the manuscript.

claim: TTP recruits the CCR4-NOT decapping and deadenylation complex to target mRNAs, resulting in their destabilization and removal from the cell.
source: Subsequently, TTP recruits the CCR4-NOT decapping and deadenylation complex to target mRNAs, resulting in their destabilization and removal from the cell (Fabian et al., 2013; Lai et al., 2003; Lykke-Andersen and Wagner, 2005; Sandler et al., 2011; Tiedje et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Not all mRNAs that TTP binds to are destabilized.
source: TTP binds to the AREs of a multitude of mRNAs encoding cytokines and other immune-related factors, yet not all of them are destabilized (Moore et al., 2018; Sedlyarov et al., 2016; Tiedje et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Zfp36-deficient mice develop systemic inflammation characterized by arthritis, dermatitis, conjunctivitis, and cachexia.
source: The biological importance of TTP for proper dampening of the inflammatory response is underpinned by the observation that Zfp36 (the gene encoding TTP)-deficient mice develop systemic inflammation characterized by arthritis, dermatitis, conjunctivitis, and cachexia, which has been coined TTP deficiency syndrome (Taylor et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: TNF mRNA is one of the main deregulated ARE-containing mRNAs driving the inflammatory phenotype in Zfp36-deficient mice.
source: One of the main deregulated ARE-containing mRNAs driving the inflammatory phenotype in Zfp36-deficient mice is Tnf (Carballo et al., 1998; Taylor et al., 1996)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Il1a/b, Il23, and Ccl3 have been implicated in the inflammatory phenotype of Zfp36-deficient mice.
source: although additionally Il1a/b, Il23, and Ccl3 have been implicated as well (Kang et al., 2011; Molle et al., 2013; Sneezum et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Zfp36 mRNA transcription is robustly induced by proinflammatory stimuli including LPS in myeloid cells such as macrophages.
source: Most cell types express low levels of Zfp36 mRNA in unstimulated conditions, the transcription of which is robustly induced by proinflammatory stimuli including the Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) agonist lipopolysaccharide (LPS) in myeloid cells such as macrophages (Carballo et al., 1998; Lai et al., 1995; Sauer et al., 2006; Schaljo et al., 2009; Suzuki et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: TTP is phosphorylated at over 30 residues by inflammation-activated stress kinases.
source: At the post-translational level, TTP is phosphorylated at over 30 residues by inflammation-activated stress kinases (Brook et al., 2006; Clark and Dean, 2016; Hitti et al., 2006; Ronkina et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Phosphorylation of TTP at residues S52 and S178 is mediated by the inflammation-activated kinase MK2.
source: Most characterized are phosphorylation events at residues S52 and S178 in murine TTP that are mediated by the inflammation-activated kinase MK2, which acts down-stream of p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK; Brook et al., 2006; Hitti et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: TTP mutants lacking S52 and S178 phosphorylation sites are highly unstable and rapidly degraded, yet highly biologically active in mice.
source: In mice, TTP mutants lacking these phosphorylation sites are highly unstable and rapidly degraded, yet highly biologically active (Ross et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: TTP is predominantly unphosphorylated and rapidly degraded in unstimulated cells.
source: This has given rise to a model in which TTP is predominantly unphosphorylated and rapidly degraded in unstimulated cells
evidence: This claim is based on inference from published literature and represents a model.

claim: Pro-inflammatory cell signaling increases Zfp36 transcription and TTP S52/S178 phosphorylation and stabilization through interaction with 14-3-3 proteins.
source: whereas pro-inflammatory cell signaling not only increases Zfp36 transcription, but also TTP S52/S178 phosphorylation and stabilization through interaction with 14-3-3 proteins (Kratochvill et al., 2011; Sedlyarov et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In the S52/S178 phosphorylated state, TTP is thought to be inactive.
source: However, in this S52/S178 phosphorylated state, TTP is thought to be inactive
evidence: This claim represents a model based on published literature.

claim: During dephosphorylation of S52/S178 at later times in the inflammatory response, TTP actively mediates mRNA degradation.
source: whereas during dephosphorylation of these residues at later times in the inflammatory response, TTP actively mediates mRNA degradation (Kratochvill et al., 2011; Sedlyarov et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Proteasomes are the main degradation machines of cells for homeostatic protein turn-over.
source: Proteasomes are the main degradation machines of cells for homeostatic protein turn-over (Bard et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: 26S proteasomes are considered the main degradative entities for poly-ubiquitinated proteins.
source: Association of 19S regulatory particles containing ubiquitin receptors and AAA+ ATPase activity assembles 26S proteasomes, which are considered the main degradative entities for poly-ubiquitinated proteins (Bard et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: TTP protein is degraded through the proteasome.
source: TTP protein is degraded through the proteasome, as previous studies showed that 20S proteasome inhibition stabilizes TTP.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A previous study suggested that TTP may be directly degraded by 20S proteasomes in a ubiquitin-independent manner.
source: Moreover, a previous study suggested that TTP may be directly degraded by 20S proteasomes in a ubiquitin-independent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Important destabilizing intrinsically disordered regions in the N and C termini of TTP have been identified.
source: In this context, important destabilizing intrinsically disordered regions in the N and C termini of TTP were identified and have been suggested to putatively allow direct degradation by 20S proteasomes (Brook et al., 2006; Ngoc et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Endogenous TTP protein was rapidly induced by LPS.
source: Consistent with previous studies, endogenous TTP protein was rapidly induced by LPS (Carballo et al., 1998; Lai et al., 1995; Sauer et al., 2006; Schaljo et al., 2009; Suzuki et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and citations to published literature.

claim: In the absence of de novo protein synthesis, TTP is rapidly degraded.
source: and in the absence of de novo protein synthesis, rapidly degraded (Figure 1A; Brook et al., 2006; Ngoc et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and citations to published literature.

claim: Treatment with proteasome inhibitor MG132 almost completely prevented TTP degradation.
source: Treatment with proteasome inhibitor MG132 almost completely prevented TTP degradation, indicating that its degradation is predominantly through the proteasome.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Under proteasome inhibition conditions, a high-MW form of TTP accumulated, suggesting that phosphorylation is important for regulation of its stability.
source: Under these conditions, a high-MW form of TTP accumulated, suggesting that phosphorylation is important for regulation of its stability.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and represents an inference from the observed molecular weight shift.

claim: LPS stimulation resulted in rapid TTP stabilization after 30 min, followed by a reduction of its protein levels at 3 hr and 7 hr post-treatment.
source: Stimulation with LPS resulted in rapid TTP stabilization after 30 min, followed by a reduction of its protein levels at 3 hr and 7 hr post-treatment (Figure 1B; lanes 2–3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Pro-inflammatory stimuli may provide the signaling required for TTP turn-over at longer stimulation times, possibly through regulating its phosphorylation.
source: This suggested that pro-inflammatory stimuli may also provide the signaling required for TTP turn-over at longer stimulation times, possibly through regulating its phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Treatment with the ubiquitin E1 inhibitor TAK-243 stabilized endogenous and exogenously expressed TTP under baseline and LPS-stimulated conditions.
source: This stabilized endogenous and exogenously expressed TTP under baseline and LPS-stimulated conditions (Figure 1B, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: TTP is degraded in a ubiquitination-dependent manner.
source: demonstrating that TTP is degraded in a ubiquitination-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from E1 inhibitor experiments.

claim: Exogenous HA-TTP and endogenous TTP was detected to be ubiquitinated in denaturing lysates.
source: Consistent with this notion, exogenous HA-TTP and endogenous TTP was detected to be ubiquitinated in denaturing lysates from these cells (Figure 1C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: A TTP mutant in which all five lysine residues in the TTP zinc finger domain were mutated to arginines (KtoR) accumulated at high steady-state levels and was substantially less ubiquitinated.
source: Moreover, a TTP mutant in which all of its five lysine residues in the TTP zinc finger domain were mutated to arginines (KtoR), accumulated at high steady-state levels, and was substantially less ubiquitinated (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The KtoR TTP mutant was stabilized.
source: Consistent with its strongly reduced ubiquitination, the KtoR TTP mutant was stabilized (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Mutation of individual lysines had no significant effects on TTP accumulation.
source: Mutation of individual lysines had no significant effects on TTP accumulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Multiple lysine residues in TTP may be functionally redundant for its ubiquitination and degradation.
source: suggesting that multiple lysine residues in TTP may be functionally redundant for its ubiquitination and degradation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the lysine mutant data.

claim: A TTP mutant with simultaneous mutation of four residues (K97/115/133/135 R) did significantly accumulate, albeit to a lesser extent than a mutant in which all five lysines were mutated.
source: A TTP mutant with simultaneous mutation of four residues (K97/115/133/135 R) did significantly accumulate, albeit to a lesser extent than a mutant in which all five lysines were mutated (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Degradative K48-linked poly-ubiquitin chains were detected on TTP.
source: In line with lysine poly-ubiquitination playing an important role in TTP degradation, degradative K48-linked poly-ubiquitin chains were detected on TTP, whereas non-degradative K63-linked chains were not (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Non-degradative K63-linked poly-ubiquitin chains were not detected on TTP.
source: In line with lysine poly-ubiquitination playing an important role in TTP degradation, degradative K48-linked poly-ubiquitin chains were detected on TTP, whereas non-degradative K63-linked chains were not (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: TTP is covalently poly-ubiquitinated in its TTP zinc finger domain.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that TTP is covalently poly-ubiquitinated in its TTP zinc finger domain
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ubiquitination and mutant studies.

claim: All five lysines in the TTP zinc finger domain are functionally important for TTP degradation.
source: and that all five lysines are functionally important for TTP degradation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from lysine mutant studies.

claim: mCherry-TTP accumulated in cells as a stable protein under non-stimulated conditions.
source: mCherry-TTP accumulated in cells as a stable protein under non-stimulated conditions (Figure 1E; top panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: LPS stimulation initially further stabilized mCherry-TTP, yet subsequently facilitated its degradation.
source: In contrast, LPS stimulation initially further stabilized mCherry-TTP, yet subsequently facilitated its degradation, phenocopying its endogenous TTP counterpart (Figure 1E; bottom panel, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Treatment of lysates with alkaline phosphatase collapsed higher migrating endogenous and exogenous TTP species.
source: Treatment of lysates from these cells with alkaline phosphatase collapsed higher migrating endogenous and exogenous TTP species (Figure 1F)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Inhibition of the phosphatases PP1 and PP2 by okadaic acid increased higher migrating TTP species.
source: whereas inhibition of the phosphatases PP1 and PP2 by okadaic acid (OA) increased them (Figure 1G)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: mCherry-TTP is phosphorylated in a similar fashion as endogenous TTP.
source: indicating that mCherry-TTP is phosphorylated in a similar fashion as endogenous TTP.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the phosphatase treatment data.

claim: LPS-stimulation initially stabilizes TTP.
source: Together, these data show that LPS-stimulation initially stabilizes TTP
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from multiple figures.

claim: At later time points, LPS-induced cell signaling events direct TTP degradation.
source: whereas at later time points its induced cell signaling events direct TTP degradation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from multiple figures.

claim: Factors previously reported to be important for stabilizing TTP (e.g. Mapkapk2 (Mk2), Ywhag (14-3-3γ), Mapk14 (p38)) were significantly enriched in the mCherry-TTPlow cell pool.
source: As anticipated, factors previously reported to be important for stabilizing TTP (e.g. Mapkapk2 (Mk2), Ywhag (14-3-3γ), Mapk14 (p38)) were significantly enriched in the mCherry-TTPlow cell pool (Figure 2—source data 6, Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; left and top panels, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the genetic screen shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Key factors for TLR4-signaling (Tlr4, Ly96 (Md2)), and components of the proteasome (Psma5, Psmb7) were significantly enriched in mCherry-TTPhigh sorted cells.
source: Consistent with mCherry-TTP proteasomal degradation being LPS-dependent (Figure 1E), key factors for TLR4-signaling (Tlr4, Ly96 (Md2)), and components of the proteasome (Psma5, Psmb7) were significantly enriched in mCherry-TTPhigh sorted cells (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; right and bottom panels, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the genetic screen shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The giant ubiquitin E3 ligase Huwe1 was identified as a regulator of TTP abundance in the genetic screen.
source: Moreover, various additional new candidates controlling cellular TTP abundance were identified, including the giant ubiquitin E3 ligase Huwe1 (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, right and top panels, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the genetic screen shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Individual targeting of screen candidates increased endogenous TTP and exogenous mCherry-TTP protein levels by western blot.
source: Individual targeting of these candidates increased endogenous TTP and exogenous mCherry-TTP protein levels by western blot (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: HUWE1 was identified as a strong determinant of endogenous and exogenous TTP protein abundance by western blot.
source: In particular, HUWE1 was identified as a strong determinant of endogenous and exogenous TTP protein abundance by western blot (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; compare LPS-treated samples)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: HUWE1 was identified as a strong determinant of endogenous TTP protein abundance by flow cytometry.
source: and flow cytometry (Figure 2D)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Huwe1 knock-out did not affect Zfp36 mRNA levels.
source: without affecting Zfp36 mRNA levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Inducible Huwe1 knock-out significantly increased endogenous TTP protein levels at later time points post-LPS stimulation.
source: Consistent with an increase in protein stability, inducible Huwe1 knock-out significantly increased endogenous TTP protein levels at later time points post-LPS stimulation (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Huwe1 knock-out did not affect LPS-induced degradation of mCherry-IκBα by flow cytometry.
source: Huwe1 knock-out increased TTP protein levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E; top panel), but did neither affect LPS-induced degradation of mCherry-IκBα by flow cytometry (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E; bottom panel)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Huwe1 knock-out did not affect endogenous IκBα degradation by western blot.
source: nor endogenous IκBα by western blot (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The Huwe1 knock-out does not affect cell signaling between TLR4 and IκBα.
source: This shows that the Huwe1 knock-out does not affect cell signaling between TLR4 and IκBα, and this does not contribute to TTP stabilization in Huwe1-deficient cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the IκBα degradation data.

claim: HUWE1 knock-out in RKO cells strongly increased TTP protein levels.
source: Similar to the phenotype in RAW264.7 cells, HUWE1 knock-out in RKO cells strongly increased TTP protein levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: HUWE1 has a similar role in human, non-myeloid cells independent of the TLR4 axis.
source: indicating that HUWE1 has a similar role in human, non-myeloid cells independent of the TLR4 axis.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the RKO cell data.

claim: Targeting of Huwe1 in mouse bone marrow derived macrophages (BMDMs) strongly increased high and low molecular weight species of endogenous TTP.
source: Moreover, targeting of Huwe1 in mouse bone marrow derived macrophages (BMDMs), likewise strongly increased high and low molecular weight species of endogenous TTP (Figure 2F)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The biological importance of Huwe1 for TTP abundance is relevant in primary cells.
source: indicating that the biological importance of Huwe1 for TTP abundance is relevant in primary cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the BMDM data.

claim: Endogenous TTP was stabilized ≥5-fold in the absence of Huwe1 (estimated half-life of ~20 hr), compared to sgROSA cells in which TTP half-life was measured to be 3.7 hr.
source: Endogenous TTP was stabilized ≥5-fold in the absence of Huwe1 (estimated half-life of ~20 hr), compared to sgROSA cells in which TTP half-life was measured to be 3.7 hr (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Huwe1 knock-out increased HA-TTP protein half-life by 83% from 35 min to 55 min.
source: In similar stability assessments with exogenously expressed TTP in the absence of LPS, Huwe1 knock-out increased HA-TTP protein half-life by 83% from 35 min to 55 min (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Loss of Huwe1 increases TTP protein half-life.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that loss of Huwe1 increases TTP protein half-life
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from half-life measurements.

claim: HUWE1 is a strong, conserved regulator of TTP protein stability.
source: and positioned HUWE1 as a strong, conserved regulator of TTP protein stability.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from multiple cell types and species.

claim: Huwe1 knock-out did not alter baseline Tnf mRNA levels.
source: Consistent with the fact that non-stimulated cells have very low levels of TTP, Huwe1 knock-out did not alter baseline Tnf (Figure 3A, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Huwe1 knock-out did not alter baseline Il6 mRNA levels.
source: or Il6 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B/C) mRNA levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B/C.

claim: Loss of Huwe1 resulted in significantly decreased concentrations of Tnf and Il6 transcripts at 3–16 hr post-stimulation.
source: Loss of Huwe1 resulted in significantly decreased concentrations of Tnf and Il6 transcripts at 3–16 hr post-stimulation (Figure 3A, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Huwe1-loss only altered mature Tnf mRNA concentrations, whereas its pre-mRNA levels remained unaffected.
source: In line with TTP-dependent post-transcriptional effects, Huwe1-loss only altered mature Tnf mRNA concentrations, whereas its pre-mRNA levels remained unaffected (Figure 3B)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Tnf transcription was likely unaffected by Huwe1 loss.
source: indicating that Tnf transcription was likely unaffected.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the pre-mRNA data.

claim: No differences in F4/80 surface expression were measured between sgROSA and sgHuwe1 BMDMs.
source: Neither did any differences stem from altered macrophage differentiation from bone marrow, as no differences in F4/80 surface expression were measured between sgROSA and sgHuwe1 BMDMs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Actinomycin D mRNA chase experiments indicated that the decreased levels of pro-inflammatory mRNAs are consistent with a 57% decrease in Tnf mRNA stability.
source: Instead, Actinomycin D mRNA chase experiments indicated that the decreased levels of pro-inflammatory mRNAs are consistent with a 57% decrease in Tnf mRNA stability (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Targeting of Zfp36 in Huwe1-deficient cells partially rescued Tnf mRNA concentrations.
source: Moreover, targeting of Zfp36 in Huwe1-deficient cells partially rescued Tnf mRNA concentrations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The effects of Huwe1 loss on Tnf mRNA levels are at least in part TTP-dependent.
source: indicating that the effects of Huwe1 loss on Tnf mRNA levels are at least in part TTP-dependent.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the Zfp36 rescue experiment.

claim: The decreased Tnf mRNA levels in Huwe1 KO cells were matched by significantly decreased intracellular TNF protein.
source: Lastly, measurements of intracellular cytokines by flow-cytometry showed that the decreased Tnf mRNA levels in Huwe1 KO cells, were matched by significantly decreased intracellular TNF protein (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Loss of Huwe1 increases the bio-active pool of cellular TTP, resulting in enhanced turn-over of TTP target mRNAs encoding pro-inflammatory mediators.
source: Taken together, these data show that loss of Huwe1 increases the bio-active pool of cellular TTP, resulting in enhanced turn-over of TTP target mRNAs encoding pro-inflammatory mediators.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the mRNA and protein data.

claim: Neither co-IP, nor TurboID proximity labeling assays identified complex formation between TTP and HUWE1 in cells.
source: Neither co-IP, nor TurboID proximity labeling assays identified complex formation between TTP and HUWE1 in cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I/J).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I/J.

claim: The effects of HUWE1 on TTP may be indirect.
source: This suggested that the effects of HUWE1 on TTP may be indirect
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the lack of interaction data.

claim: The effect of Huwe1 loss on TTP stability was predominantly at time points after the initial two hours of LPS stimulation.
source: Data from Huwe1 knock-out cells indicated that the effect of Huwe1 loss on TTP stability was predominantly at time points after the initial two hours of LPS stimulation (Figure 2E)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Huwe1 ablation did not significantly alter the total protein levels or change the early phosphorylation/activation kinetics of stress kinases p38, MK2, ERK, and JNK between 0 and 60 min post-LPS treatment.
source: Consistent with this finding, Huwe1 ablation did not significantly alter the total protein levels or change the early phosphorylation/activation kinetics of stress kinases p38, MK2, ERK, and JNK between 0 and 60 min post-LPS treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: Ablation of Huwe1 strongly increased endogenous TTP levels upon its induction by LPS at all measured later time points from 2 to 16 hr post-stimulation.
source: In contrast, ablation of Huwe1 strongly increased endogenous TTP levels upon its induction by LPS at all measured later time points from 2 to 16 hr post-stimulation (Figures 2E and 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2E and 4A.

claim: Huwe1-targeting consistently increased the activated phosphorylated forms of all kinases at 2 hr post-stimulation.
source: In contrast, Huwe1-targeting consistently increased the activated phosphorylated forms of all kinases at 2 hr post-stimulation (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A–D.

claim: MK2 and JNK activation was increased for prolonged times, up to 6 hr post-stimulation in Huwe1-targeted cells.
source: While activated p38 and ERK levels in Huwe1-targeted cells were comparable to the ROSA-targeted control, or even lower, at later time points (Figure 4A–C), MK2 and JNK activation was increased for prolonged times, up to 6 hr post-stimulation (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B–D.

claim: In the absence of LPS stimulation, Huwe1 knock-out did not affect, or even decreased, baseline phosphorylated levels of all kinases.
source: Importantly, in the absence of LPS stimulation, Huwe1 knock-out did not affect, or even decreased, baseline phosphorylated levels of all kinases (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A–D.

claim: Huwe1 ablation in the presence of LPS did not induce unrelated stress responses, such as p53 activation.
source: Moreover, Huwe1 ablation in the presence of LPS did not induce unrelated stress responses, such as p53 activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Loss of Huwe1 does not induce a general stress response in the cell, but is specific for pro-inflammatory cellular conditions mediated by LPS.
source: indicating that loss of Huwe1 does not induce a general stress response in the cell, but is specific for pro-inflammatory cellular conditions mediated by LPS.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the p53 activation data.

claim: In the absence of Huwe1, multiple stress kinases may be activated more, and for prolonged times.
source: Together, these data indicated that in the absence of Huwe1, multiple stress kinases may be activated more, and for prolonged times.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the kinase activation data.

claim: Treatment of sgROSA-targeted cells with p38 or MK2 inhibitors significantly decreased TTP levels.
source: In line with previous reports that the p38-MK2 axis is an important determinant of TTP stability, treatment of sgROSA-targeted cells with p38 or MK2 inhibitors significantly decreased TTP levels (Figure 4E; sample sets 4 and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Simultaneous Huwe1 knock-out still elevated TTP levels in the presence of p38 or MK2 inhibitors.
source: However, simultaneous Huwe1 knock-out still elevated TTP levels in the presence of these individual inhibitors
